walkthrough:
**Recall the ideal gas assumptions**

Think side by side with me. An ideal gas assumes two things. Particles have negligible volume and have no intermolecular forces.

Ideal gas obeys:
$$pV = nRT$$

**Why high temperature helps**

At high temperature, particles move very fast with large kinetic energy. This energy easily overcomes any weak London forces between $\text{N}_2$ molecules, so they behave as if no forces exist.

**Why low pressure helps**

At low pressure, the gas is very spread out. The distance between molecules is huge, so the volume of the molecules themselves is negligible and attractions are almost zero.

**Put it together**

Most ideal means hottest and most spread out. That is high temperature combined with low pressure, which lets nitrogen follow $pV = nRT$ most closely.

options.A: This is the opposite of ideal. Low temperature lets intermolecular forces matter and high pressure squeezes molecules close together, so both particle volume and attractions cause large deviations.
options.B: This is correct. High temperature overcomes attractions with high kinetic energy, and low pressure keeps molecules far apart so their volume is negligible. Both assumptions of the ideal gas model are best met.
options.C: Low pressure is good, but low temperature is not. When cold, $\text{N}_2$ molecules move slowly and London forces can hold them together, even leading toward liquefaction, so it deviates from ideal.
options.D: High temperature is good, but high pressure is not. When compressed, molecules are forced close together so the volume of the particles and the forces between them are no longer negligible.
